title: KM 算法与 Hall 定理

text: Labels, tight edges, slack; |N(S)| ≥ |S|.

Maximum-weight perfect matching in a bipartite graph with n + n vertices: the KM algorithm (Kuhn– Munkres, 匈牙利算法的带权版本) keeps labels lx[i] (left) and ly[j] (right) with lx[i] + ly[j] ≥ w(i, j) for every edge. Edges with equality are "tight"; a perfect matching using only tight edges is optimal. When the search for an augmenting path gets stuck, lower lx on the visited left vertices and raise ly on the visited right ones by the smallest slack, which creates a new tight edge.

The BFS version with slack[j] = min over visited i of lx[i] + ly[j] − w(i, j) runs in O(n³) (P6577). Min-cost flow (拓展篇第1章) solves the same problem more slowly but more flexibly; KM is the tool when n ≤ 500 and the graph is complete or dense.

The DFS version of KM is O(n⁴) on bad inputs; use the BFS-with-slack version above. For a maximum- weight matching that need not be perfect, add zero-weight dummy edges first.

Hall's theorem (Hall 定理): a bipartite graph has a matching covering every left vertex iff every set S of left vertices has |N(S)| ≥ |S| (at least as many neighbours). It turns matching questions into inequalities that can be checked with data structures.

Ice Skates (P3488): people of shoe size i may take skates of sizes i … i + d. Hall's condition only needs to be checked on contiguous size ranges: Σl..r (people − k) ≤ k·d for all l ≤ r, i.e. the maximum subarray sum of (counti − k) ≤ k·d, a segment tree with maximum subarray nodes (进阶篇第6章) under point updates.
Layered BFS; disjoint shortest paths; O(m√n).

Hopcroft–Karp: instead of one augmenting path at a time (Hungarian / Kuhn, O(nm)), each phase BFS- layers the graph from all free left vertices, then finds a maximal set of vertex-disjoint shortest augmenting paths by DFS along the layers. There are only O(√n) phases, so the total is O(m√n).
It is Dinic on the unit-capacity matching network written directly. Use it when n is large (10⁵) and Kuhn is too slow (P3386 in its big-data variants).
Checked against Kuhn's algorithm in Python on a random bipartite graph.
Gale–Shapley proposals; proposer-optimal.

Stable marriage (稳定婚姻 , Gale–Shapley): n men and n women each rank the other side. A matching is stable if no man and woman both prefer each other to their partners. Free men propose down their lists; a woman keeps the best proposer so far and rejects the rest. It ends after at most n² proposals with a stable matching.

The result is proposer-optimal: every man gets the best partner he has in any stable matching (and every woman the worst). P1407 asks the related question whether a given marriage is "unsafe" (an alternating cycle exists), solved with SCC.

Key points to memorise
1. KM: labels lx + ly ≥ w; tight edges equal; perfect tight matching = optimal.
2. Stuck: change labels by the smallest slack; BFS version O(n³).
3. Hall: left side fully matchable ⇔ |N(S)| ≥ |S| for every S.
4. Hopcroft–Karp: BFS layers from free left vertices, DFS disjoint shortest paths; O(√n) phases.
5. Gale–Shapley: free men propose in order; women keep the best; ≤ n² proposals.
